data.content_ref: inline:The target's defense collapses because it conflates 'logical aim' with 'rational basis for action.' Popper explicitly rejects the principle of induction, yet the target admits the agent has 'no rational assurance' the theory will work. If there is no rational link between past severity and future performance, then preferring the better-corroborated theory over a worse one (or a random guess) for practical action (like building a bridge) becomes an arbitrary act of faith, not a defensible methodological rule. The target fails to explain why severity provides a *reason* to act if it provides no expectation of success, thereby smuggling in an implicit inductive assumption that 'what worked before is a better guide than what didn't,' which contradicts the core anti-inductive stance it claims to defend.
